title: Doing nothing, nothing undone
hookLine: the Tao does nothing, yet nothing is left undone (Tao Te Ching 37)

lines: A WEEK GATHERED INTO ONE SENTENCE.
cards: Bread dough, under a towel on the counter. All afternoon, nobody touches it. Nobody kneads, nobody checks, nobody helps.
And when the towel comes off, it has swelled over the rim of the bowl.

This week's chapters kept circling that kind of thing: the army whose thorns outlast its win, the victor who mourns, streams finding the sea, the mirror turned back on yourself, the flood that claims nothing, the plain taste, the soft door.
Chapter thirty-seven gathers it into one sentence, and today's word is the first half of it.

teach.h: DOES NOTHING, AND NOTHING IS UNDONE.
teach.b: First, the sentence. In James Legge's translation: "The Tao in its regular course does nothing (for the sake of doing it), and so there is nothing which it does not do."
Doing nothing there is wu wei, the word you met early on this path: acting without forcing. Look at Legge's parentheses. He's warning the reader: this isn't laziness.
The Tao isn't asleep. It just doesn't do things for the sake of doing them, doesn't push, doesn't fuss. And somehow, nothing is left undone.
The chapter says if rulers could hold on to this, all things would transform by themselves. Not be transformed by a decree. Transform, on their own, the way dough rises.
Third, when wanting stirs. The chapter admits that even in that quiet, desire starts to rise up again: the urge to step in, to improve, to manage.
Its answer is to settle that urge with the nameless simplicity, the same uncarved plainness from chapter twenty-eight. Fourth, stillness.
The chapter ends: without desire, there is stillness, and the world settles itself. Tradition treats this chapter as the close of the book's first part, the part about the Tao.

teach.h: NOTHING WHICH IT DOES NOT DO.
teach.b: Tomorrow the second part begins. In a household or an office, the opposite looks like the parent hovering over the homework, the manager rewriting every email, the gardener tugging seedlings to help them grow.
Sometimes the useful thing is to set things up well and take your hands off. The bread doesn't need you watching it.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty-seven's 'doing nothing' as not forcing: setting things up well, then letting them unfold without constant interference.

o: being lazy and avoiding all work and duty
not forcing, so that nothing is left undone
refusing to help so others learn on their own

p: does nothing, and nothing is undone
all things would transform by themselves

s: doing nothing in chapter thirty-seven means being lazy
Legge adds 'for the sake of doing it': the Tao doesn't force or fuss, and nothing is left undone.
the chapter says that with stillness, the world settles itself
without desire there is stillness, and things settle on their own.
tradition treats chapter thirty-seven as the close of the book's first part
the part about the Tao; the second part begins with the next chapter.

games.q: a seedling is coming up slower than you'd like. what would chapter thirty-seven's Tao do?
o: tug it up a little each day to help.
water it, then leave it to grow.
dig it up to check the roots.
games.why: the Tao does nothing for the sake of doing it, and nothing is left undone. the chapter says things transform by themselves.

practice: Start with the breath: don't do it, let it happen, the in-breath coming without being called and the out-breath leaving without a push. Then think of one thing you've been hovering over, a project, a person, a plan.
Picture it set on the counter under a towel, not abandoned, just left to rise on its own for a while.

wordCard.voice: Doing nothing. The first half of chapter thirty-seven's sentence: the Tao does nothing for the sake of doing it, and so there is nothing it does not do. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: non-doing, not forcing; the heart of chapter thirty-seven's sentence.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing undone. Hands off isn't the same as giving up. That's the week.
